items.abstract: <jats:p>Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are no longer a research curiosity-they are being deployed in production environments across industries. Yet for all the progress in what these systems can do, comparatively little attention has been paid to how, and under what conditions, they break. This paper attempts to fill part of that gap. Drawing on over forty published works from 2020 through early 2025, I propose a four-dimensional taxonomy of LLM agent failure modes, organized around the core functional modules present in most agentic architectures: reasoning and planning, tool use and action execution, memory and context management, and multi-agent orchestration. For each dimension, I provide formal definitions of specific failure classes, describe triggering conditions, and supply concrete illustrative examples grounded in the empirical literature. I also introduce the Agent Robustness Evaluation Protocol (AREP)-a lightweight, framework-agnostic robustness evaluation methodology intended to surface latent failure risks before deployment rather than after. The paper concludes with seven practitioner recommendations for building agentic systems that are not merely capable, but meaningfully robust and reliable.</jats:p>
title: Why AI Agents Fail: A Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Autonomous LLM-Based Systems

items.abstract: Current multi-agent LLM systems difffferentiate agents through hand-crafted roles or layer-stacking architectures. We propose Agora, a framework that difffferentiates agents through six continuous drives (boredom, curiosity, stress, anxiety, empathy, service) that map to LLM parameters, producing parameter-level difffferentiation without prompt engineering. We evaluate Agora through 375 real API calls on DeepSeek Chat across four task types, comparing RoundTable (3 difffferentiated agents) against four baselines: Single, MajorityVoting, BestOf3, and AutoGenStyle. Results reveal a task-dependent pattern: RoundTable produces signifificantly higher quality on analytical tasks (p < 0.001 vs AutoGenStyle, Cohen’s d = 2.26) but does not outperform simpler baselines on creative tasks (MajorityVoting wins, p < 0.001) or short-format generation (AutoGenStyle wins, p = 0.006). Closed-loop drive-LLM integration maintained stable quality over 20 consecutive steps. Ablations identify empathy as the most critical drive component. These results suggest that drive-based difffferentiation shows promise for an-alytical reasoning tasks, outperforming some multi-agent baselines (AutoGenStyle, BestOf3) with large effffect sizes, though the comparison against a single difffferentiated agent does not reach signifificance. Simpler coordination strategies remain competitive for creative generation. We discuss the implications for multi-agent LLM system design and identify directions for future work.
title: Agora: A Drive-Based Framework for Agent Difffferentiation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
